title: Impromptu and Extemporaneous Speaking
summary: Speaking with little preparation is a skill you can practice: a simple structure, a few examples you can reach for, and a steady habit of reading the news.

p: **Impromptu** speaking means getting a topic (a quotation, a word, an object, a question) and speaking about it after only a few minutes of preparation. **Extemporaneous** speaking ("extemp") means choosing one of three current-events questions, preparing for 30 minutes with files of articles you gathered beforehand (no internet), and giving a speech of up to seven minutes from memory, in the National Speech & Debate Association's version. Both are offered at many speech tournaments; time limits vary by league.
Even if you never enter either event, the skill helps every debater. Rebuttals, crossfire, parliamentary prep and World Schools impromptu motions are all speaking with little preparation.

sections.h: A structure you can use anywhere
ol: **Hook**: a quick story, fact or question that relates to the topic.
**Conclusion**: restate the thesis and tie back to the hook.
p: Under time pressure, two well-developed points beat three rushed ones.

list: Spend the first part choosing your thesis. Don't start writing until you know your answer.
Write only a few words per point, big enough to see at a glance.
Pick examples from your mental "bank": a historical event, a book, a science fact, a personal experience, a current event.
Leave a few seconds to say your first sentence in your head.

p: Good impromptu speakers aren't making things up on the spot; they're drawing on what they already know. Keep a notebook of examples that fit many topics: a few historical events, a few people who changed their minds, a few scientific discoveries, a few books. The [Harvard Classics daily reading](/harvard-classics/) and the [timeline](/timeline/) are good places to fill it.

list: Read news from several sources with different points of view every week.
Keep files by topic (economy, foreign policy, technology) so you can find articles quickly.
Answer the exact question you drew; don't give a prepared speech on a nearby topic.
Cite sources by name and date: "According to a Federal Reserve report from March...".

example.title: Topic: "Is it better to be a leader or a good teammate?" (one minute of prep)

lines.s: In a relay race, the anchor gets the cheers, but the race is won by four runners.
Being a good teammate comes first, because good leaders are made from it.
Teams need people who do their part without the spotlight. Example: a debate partner who researches the cards the other one reads.
Most people trusted to lead earned it by being reliable teammates. Example: a team captain chosen by her teammates.
So run your leg well. Sometimes that's what makes you the anchor.

practice: Use the impromptu prep timer in the drills: draw a topic, prepare for one or two minutes, speak for three.
Fill a page of your example bank with five examples you could use on many topics.
Read one news story a day from a source you don't usually read, and summarize it in two sentences.
